title: 06. Typing & Models: Enum Types
summary: Python provides several specialized Enum types for different use cases:

sections.title: Concept Explanation (Junior Developer Style)
sections.body:
Python provides several **specialized Enum types** for different use cases:

```
Enum      → Base class. Members can be anything.
IntEnum   → Members ARE integers. Support int operations.
StrEnum   → Members ARE strings. Support string operations. (3.11+)
Flag      → Members can be COMBINED with | (bitwise OR).
IntFlag   → Flag + integer support.
auto()    → Python auto-assigns values.
```

> 🧠 Think of the different Enum types like **different types of labels** 🏷️:
>
> - `Enum` = custom label (no built-in operations)
> - `IntEnum` = label that IS a number (can do math with it)
> - `StrEnum` = label that IS a string (can use as string directly)
> - `Flag` = label that can be COMBINED (like permissions)

sections.title: 5 Examples
sections.body:
```python
# ── Example 1: IntEnum — integer-valued enum ──────────────────────────
from enum import Enum, IntEnum

# Regular Enum — NOT equal to integers
class RegularPriority(Enum):
    LOW    = 1
    MEDIUM = 2
    HIGH   = 3

print(f"Enum == 1 : {RegularPriority.LOW == 1}")   # False!
print(f"Enum  > 1 : {RegularPriority.HIGH > 1}")    # TypeError!... let's try:
try:
    print(RegularPriority.HIGH > RegularPriority.LOW)
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"Can't compare regular Enum: {e}")

# IntEnum — behaves like int + enum
class Priority(IntEnum):
    LOW      = 1
    MEDIUM   = 2
    HIGH     = 3
    CRITICAL = 4

print(f"\nIntEnum == 1: {Priority.LOW == 1}")         # True!
print(f"IntEnum  > 2: {Priority.HIGH > 2}")            # True!
print(f"IntEnum sort: {sorted([Priority.HIGH, Priority.LOW, Priority.MEDIUM])}")
# [<Priority.LOW: 1>, <Priority.MEDIUM: 2>, <Priority.HIGH: 3>]

# Can use in integer contexts directly
priority_score = Priority.HIGH + 10   # works like int!
print(f"Math       : {Priority.HIGH + 10}")  # 13
print(f"Min        : {min(Priority)}")        # Priority.LOW: 1

# Real world: HTTP status codes
class HTTPStatus(IntEnum):
    OK         = 200
    CREATED    = 201
    BAD_REQUEST= 400
    NOT_FOUND  = 404
    SERVER_ERR = 500

    @property
    def is_success(self) -> bool:
        return 200 <= self.value < 300

    @property
    def is_client_error(self) -> bool:
        return 400 <= self.value < 500

status = HTTPStatus.NOT_FOUND
print(f"\n{status.name}: is_success={status.is_success}, "
      f"is_client_error={status.is_client_error}")

# Works as integer in comparisons
print(f"404 is client error: {400 <= HTTPStatus.NOT_FOUND < 500}")
```

```python
# ── Example 2: StrEnum — string-valued enum (Python 3.11+) ────────────
# For earlier Python, use: class MyEnum(str, Enum)
import sys
from enum import Enum

# Python 3.11+
if sys.version_info >= (3, 11):
    from enum import StrEnum

    class Color(StrEnum):
        RED   = "red"
        GREEN = "green"
        BLUE  = "blue"

    print(f"StrEnum == 'red': {Color.RED == 'red'}")    # True!
    print(f"Upper: {Color.RED.upper()}")                  # 'RED' (string method!)
    print(f"Format: {f'Color is {Color.GREEN}'}")        # 'Color is green'

# For Python < 3.11, use (str, Enum):
class Direction(str, Enum):
    NORTH = "north"
    SOUTH = "south"
    EAST  = "east"
    WEST  = "west"

# Works as string directly!
d = Direction.NORTH
print(f"\nString operations:")
print(f"  Upper      : {d.upper()}")        # "NORTH"
print(f"  Startswith : {d.startswith('n')}") # True
print(f"  == 'north' : {d == 'north'}")      # True!
print(f"  In list    : {d in ['north','south']}") # True!

# Real world: API field names
class APIField(str, Enum):
    USER_ID    = "user_id"
    USERNAME   = "username"
    EMAIL      = "email"
    CREATED_AT = "created_at"

import json

# Works directly in dict operations!
data = {
    APIField.USER_ID:   "U001",
    APIField.USERNAME:  "alice",
    APIField.EMAIL:     "alice@example.com",
}
# Keys ARE strings, so JSON works without conversion!
print(f"\nJSON: {json.dumps(data)}")  # {"user_id": "U001", ...}

# Access like string
print(f"User ID: {data[APIField.USER_ID]}")
print(f"Same as: {data['user_id']}")  # True — same key!
```

```python
# ── Example 3: auto() — automatic value assignment ────────────────────
from enum import Enum, auto, IntEnum

# auto() assigns values automatically (1, 2, 3, ...)
class Weekday(Enum):
    MONDAY    = auto()  # 1
    TUESDAY   = auto()  # 2
    WEDNESDAY = auto()  # 3
    THURSDAY  = auto()  # 4
    FRIDAY    = auto()  # 5
    SATURDAY  = auto()  # 6
    SUNDAY    = auto()  # 7

print("Weekdays with auto():")
for day in Weekday:
    print(f"  {day.name:<12} = {day.value}")

# Custom _generate_next_value_ to control auto() behavior
class UpperCaseEnum(str, Enum):
    """auto() generates UPPERCASE string values from names"""

    @staticmethod
    def _generate_next_value_(name, start, count, last_values):
        return name.upper()  # use the member NAME as the value, uppercased

    READ   = auto()  # value = "READ"
    WRITE  = auto()  # value = "WRITE"
    DELETE = auto()  # value = "DELETE"
    ADMIN  = auto()  # value = "ADMIN"

print("\nUpperCaseEnum with custom auto():")
for p in UpperCaseEnum:
    print(f"  {p.name:<10} = {p.value!r}")

# lowercase auto
class LowerCaseEnum(str, Enum):
    @staticmethod
    def _generate_next_value_(name, start, count, last_values):
        return name.lower()

    STATUS_ACTIVE   = auto()  # "status_active"
    STATUS_INACTIVE = auto()  # "status_inactive"

print("\nLowerCaseEnum:")
for s in LowerCaseEnum:
    print(f"  {s.name:<20} = {s.value!r}")
```

```python
# ── Example 4: Flag — combinable enum (bitmask permissions) ───────────
from enum import Flag, auto, IntFlag

# Flag: members can be combined with | (bitwise OR)
class Permission(Flag):
    NONE    = 0
    READ    = auto()   # 1
    WRITE   = auto()   # 2
    DELETE  = auto()   # 4
    EXECUTE = auto()   # 8
    ADMIN   = auto()   # 16

    # Composite (combination of others)
    READ_WRITE    = READ | WRITE            # 3
    FULL_ACCESS   = READ | WRITE | DELETE | EXECUTE | ADMIN  # 31
    STANDARD_USER = READ | WRITE           # same as READ_WRITE

print("Permission values:")
for p in Permission:
    print(f"  {p.name:<15} = {p.value:>3} ({p.value:08b})")

# Combine permissions with |
user_perms = Permission.READ | Permission.WRITE
admin_perms= Permission.FULL_ACCESS

print(f"\nUser permissions : {user_perms}")
print(f"Admin permissions: {admin_perms}")

# Check permissions with in operator
print(f"\nCan read  : {Permission.READ  in user_perms}")   # True
print(f"Can delete: {Permission.DELETE in user_perms}")    # False
print(f"Can admin : {Permission.ADMIN  in admin_perms}")   # True

# Add/remove permissions
user_perms |= Permission.DELETE    # add DELETE
print(f"After adding DELETE: {user_perms}")

user_perms &= ~Permission.WRITE    # remove WRITE
print(f"After removing WRITE: {user_perms}")

# Real world: Unix file permissions
class UnixPermission(IntFlag):
    NONE      = 0
    EXEC      = 1
    WRITE     = 2
    READ      = 4
    # Combined for owner/group/other
    OWNER_ALL = READ | WRITE | EXEC    # 7  = rwx
    GROUP_READ= READ                    # 4  = r--
    OTHER_NONE= NONE                    # 0  = ---

# Like chmod 744
chmod_744 = (UnixPermission.OWNER_ALL << 6 |
             UnixPermission.GROUP_READ << 3 |
             UnixPermission.OTHER_NONE)
print(f"\nchmod 744: {oct(chmod_744)[2:]}")  # 744
```

```python
# ── Example 5: Real world — Role-Based Access Control with Flag ────────
from enum import Flag, auto, IntEnum
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict

class Permission(Flag):
    # Content permissions
    READ_CONTENT    = auto()
    WRITE_CONTENT   = auto()
    DELETE_CONTENT  = auto()
    PUBLISH_CONTENT = auto()

    # User management
    VIEW_USERS      = auto()
    MANAGE_USERS    = auto()
    DELETE_USERS    = auto()

    # System permissions
    VIEW_LOGS       = auto()
    MANAGE_SETTINGS = auto()
    MANAGE_BILLING  = auto()

    # Composite permissions (roles)
    VIEWER    = READ_CONTENT
    AUTHOR    = READ_CONTENT | WRITE_CONTENT
    EDITOR    = AUTHOR | DELETE_CONTENT | PUBLISH_CONTENT
    MODERATOR = EDITOR | VIEW_USERS
    ADMIN     = MODERATOR | MANAGE_USERS | DELETE_USERS | VIEW_LOGS
    SUPERADMIN= ADMIN | MANAGE_SETTINGS | MANAGE_BILLING

class Role(IntEnum):
    VIEWER    = 1
    AUTHOR    = 2
    EDITOR    = 3
    MODERATOR = 4
    ADMIN     = 5
    SUPERADMIN= 6

# Map roles to their permissions
ROLE_PERMISSIONS: Dict[Role, Permission] = {
    Role.VIEWER:    Permission.VIEWER,
    Role.AUTHOR:    Permission.AUTHOR,
    Role.EDITOR:    Permission.EDITOR,
    Role.MODERATOR: Permission.MODERATOR,
    Role.ADMIN:     Permission.ADMIN,
    Role.SUPERADMIN:Permission.SUPERADMIN,
}

@dataclass
class UserAccount:
    user_id:    str
    username:   str
    role:       Role
    extra_perms:Permission = Permission(0)   # additional custom permissions

    @property
    def permissions(self) -> Permission:
        """Combine role permissions + extra permissions"""
        return ROLE_PERMISSIONS[self.role] | self.extra_perms

    def can(self, permission: Permission) -> bool:
        return permission in self.permissions

    def grant(self, permission: Permission):
        """Grant additional permission beyond role"""
        self.extra_perms |= permission

    def revoke(self, permission: Permission):
        """Revoke a specific permission"""
        self.extra_perms &= ~permission

# Demo
alice = UserAccount("U001", "alice", Role.EDITOR)
bob   = UserAccount("U002", "bob",   Role.AUTHOR)

print(f"Alice ({alice.role.name}) permissions:")
for perm in Permission:
    if perm.value and perm in Permission.SUPERADMIN:  # only check basic perms
        if not any(p in perm.name for p in ["VIEWER","AUTHOR","EDITOR",
                                              "MODERATOR","ADMIN","SUPERADMIN"]):
            has = alice.can(perm)
            print(f"  {perm.name:<25}: {'✅' if has else '❌'}")

# Grant Bob extra permission
bob.grant(Permission.VIEW_USERS)  # special case
print(f"\nBob can view users: {bob.can(Permission.VIEW_USERS)}")  # True (granted)
print(f"Bob role: {bob.role.name} (normally no VIEW_USERS)")
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between Enum, IntEnum, and StrEnum?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Simply re-declare the field in the child with the same name.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Discriminated unions use a literal "discriminator" field to tell Pydantic which model to use when the input could be one of several types.
5-Year Exp Answer: > A regular Python class requires you to manually write __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and other dunder methods.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Enum is the base class — members are their own type and NOT equal to their values (Color.RED != "red", Color.RED != 1).
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Enum is the base class — members are their own type and NOT equal to their values (Color.RED != "red", Color.RED != 1). IntEnum makes members behave as integers — Status.ACTIVE == 1 is True, sorting and arithmetic work. StrEnum (3.11+) or (str, Enum) makes members behave as strings — Direction.NORTH == "north" is True, string methods work directly.

quiz.question: What is auto() and how can you customize it?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > __post_init__ is NOT automatically chained — if both parent and child define it, only the child's runs (standard Python method resolution).
5-Year Exp Answer: > Pydantic handles nested models automatically.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Four access patterns: (1) Direct — Color.RED — most common, use in code logic.
5-Year Exp Answer: > auto() automatically generates a value for an Enum member so you don't hardcode numbers.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: auto() automatically generates a value for an Enum member so you don't hardcode numbers. Default behavior: starts at 1, increments by 1. Customized by overriding _generate_next_value_(name, start, count, last_values) as a static method: name = member name, start = starting value, count = how many values assigned so far, last_values = list of previous values.

quiz.question: What is Flag and when do you use it instead of Enum?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > This is the classic Python mutable default argument bug.
5-Year Exp Answer: > A regular Python class requires you to manually write __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and other dunder methods.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Never expose raw Pydantic ValidationError to clients — transform it: > > > > Log the full error internally, return clean user-facing messages.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Flag allows members to be combined using bitwise operators (|, &, ~, ^).
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Flag allows members to be combined using bitwise operators (|, &, ~, ^). Each member is a power of 2, so any combination has a unique value. Use Flag when: (1) An entity can have multiple states simultaneously.

quiz.question: How do you iterate and filter Enum members?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Discriminated unions use a literal "discriminator" field to tell Pydantic which model to use when the input could be one of several types.
5-Year Exp Answer: > This is the classic Python mutable default argument bug.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Generic models use Python's Generic[T] to create reusable model templates parameterized by type.
5-Year Exp Answer: > > > > len(Status) gives member count. Status.__members__ is an ordered dict of all members including aliases.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: len(Status) gives member count. Status.__members__ is an ordered dict of all members including aliases. Filtering is just list comprehension over the Enum. ---

quiz.question: What are Enum aliases and how do you work with them?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > mode="before": validator runs BEFORE Pydantic's type parsing.
5-Year Exp Answer: > asdict() performs a deep recursive conversion — nested dataclasses are also converted to dicts, lists of dataclasses become lists of dicts, tuples…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Pydantic handles nested models automatically.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Enum aliases occur when two members have the same value — the second becomes an alias for the first: > > > > To prevent aliases (raise error if…
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Enum aliases occur when two members have the same value — the second becomes an alias for the first: To prevent aliases (raise error if duplicate values): use @unique decorator from enum: I always use @unique in production code — accidental aliases cause confusing behavior. The only time I intentionally use aliases is when supporting multiple names for backward compatibility. --- --- S1.
